paras: The Columbian Union Klan circular in Richmond, Virginia, was a 1919 letter calling white citizens to a masked meeting at the Business Men's Club to organize a 'new Richmond Klan' as a successor to the Ku Klux Klan of Reconstruction. The Richmond Planet published the letter on July 5, 1919, and read it as an effort to tell Black people to stay away from the city. No violence was reported, but the publication drew protest from Black ministers and returned soldiers in Richmond.

The letter came from the Columbian Union, whose letterhead gave its address as the Columbian Union Building in Nashville, Tennessee. According to the Baltimore Afro-American, the order was running a drive for members in every large Southern city and had cut its initiation fee from $50 to $10. The Planet called it the same order that Governor Bickett of North Carolina had recently 'scathingly denounced.'

The letter praised the men who 'cradled and upheld the Ku Klux Klan' during Reconstruction, even at a 'seeming disregard' of the law. It called those present at the Business Men's Club in the American National Bank Building at 8:30 p.m. on June 16 to be 'seated in the Degree of the mask,' after which officers would be elected. The Planet said the original had evidently been sent to certain white citizens and was handed to its office, but it did not know whether the meeting was held.

A week later the Planet reported that the circular had caused 'a downright sensation' in Richmond and that no one was willing to take responsibility for the meeting. Black soldiers recently returned from overseas spoke out about it, and the Baptist Ministers' Conference, meeting at Second Baptist Church, appointed a committee to ask editor John Mitchell Jr. to attend a session on what action to take. Pastors W. T. Johnson, Z. D. Lewis and T. J. King were among those named as outspoken.
No response from Mayor Ainslie, the Business Men's Club or the Chamber of Commerce appears in the coverage.

The Richmond Planet broke the story under the headline 'Klux Klan in Richmond, Virginia,' reproducing the letter in type and in facsimile. Its editorial 'What Does It Mean?' recalled that the old Klan's purposes were 'to terrorize and maltreat colored people of both sexes' and asked whether the mayor and the Director of Public Safety had been told. In shorter paragraphs the paper exclaimed 'Good Lord deliver us!', called the Klan 'a mighty poor advertisement for Richmond', and urged that if a Richmond Klan formed, Black people should organize as well. The Planet reran the editorial and the letter on July 12.

The Baltimore Afro-American took up the story on July 11, quoting the letter's hope for a 'new (Richmond) Klan' and calling the Klan 'ill-reputed bandits and night riders' rising against Black organizing for equal rights. It reported that all Richmond, white and Black, was aroused, and predicted the new Klan would be crushed in its infancy.
The Planet's editorials differed on how far the effort had gone, saying in one place that a Klan 'is being organized' in the city and in another that it was 'organized or proposed to be organized.'

reader.title: Columbian Union Klan circular in Richmond, Virginia
bases: No violence is reported; the episode is a circular calling a masked meeting to organize a 'new Richmond Klan', which the Richmond Planet read as an effort to drive Black people away (A3, A5, A7).

The Richmond meeting call is known from the Richmond Planet's reproduction of the letter (A3, A7); the Baltimore Afro-American quotes the same letter line (A9) and may depend on the Planet, though it adds details on the Nashville drive not in the Planet.

accounts.label: Columbian Union letter
accounts.gist: The letter praised the Reconstruction Klan, hoped 'the new Richmond Klan' would be its worthy successor, and called a masked meeting at the Business Men's Club for June 16 with election of officers.

accounts.label: Richmond Planet editorials
accounts.gist: The Planet said a Klan was being organized in Richmond to tell Black people to stay away and asked city officials, the Business Men's Club and the Chamber of Commerce to explain.

accounts.label: Baltimore Afro-American
accounts.gist: The Afro-American placed the Richmond effort within a Nashville-run organizing drive across Southern cities and said all Richmond was aroused.

framing.detail: The Planet headlined 'Klux Klan in Richmond, Virginia' and 'What Does It Mean?', recalled the old Klan's 'brutality and murder', and asked, 'Good Lord deliver us!'
The Afro-American called the Klan 'ill-reputed bandits and night riders' and predicted the 'new Ku Klux' would be crushed in its infancy.

versions.value: 'organized or proposed to be organized'; whether the meeting was held unknown

conflicts.note: The Planet's own editorials differ; no report shows the meeting took place.
Side detail; the Planet also printed a Raleigh dispatch on Bickett (A6).
